n0001.title: Replication crisis
n0001.gist: Science's flawed incentives and weak statistics let many published findings fail to replicate, and reform is underway.
n0001.question: Replication crisis — why do published findings often fail to replicate, and how can science fix it?

n0002.title: Introduction and definitions
n0002.gist: Replication means repeating a study to confirm its result, and researchers use statistical tests with p-values to decide whether an effect is real.
n0002.question: Replication and reproducibility — what do these terms mean and how does statistical testing decide a result holds? (background concepts)

n0003.title: Defining the crisis
n0003.gist: The replication crisis names the widespread failure to reproduce published findings, a problem now studied by metascience across psychology, medicine, and other sciences.

n0010.title: Reproducibility versus replication
n0010.gist: Researchers distinguish reproducibility, reanalyzing existing data, from replication, repeating a study with new data, and recognize direct, systematic, and conceptual replication types.

n0019.title: Judging statistical significance
n0019.gist: A hypothesis counts as supported when results are statistically significant, meaning the chance of such results occurring by pure luck falls below a chosen threshold like 5%.

n0022.title: Null hypothesis testing framework
n0022.gist: Null hypothesis testing compares a baseline assumption of no effect against an alternative using a test statistic and threshold, producing one of four possible outcomes.

n0035.title: Power and p-values
n0035.gist: Statistical power is the chance of detecting a true effect, while the p-value measures how surprising the data would be if there were truly no effect.

n0042.title: Origins of the crisis
n0042.gist: A cluster of failed replications and fraud cases in the early 2010s, building on decades of earlier warnings, turned quiet doubts into a named crisis.
n0042.question: Origins of the crisis — why did long-standing doubts about replication suddenly erupt around 2010? (a chain of events)

n0043.title: Precursor events
n0043.gist: Four episodes—failed social-priming and ESP replications, dismal biomedical replication rates, and studies exposing flexible 'p-hacking' practices—triggered the crisis in the early 2010s.

n0049.title: Naming the crisis
n0049.gist: These failures bred widespread skepticism, prompting scholars to declare a 'crisis of confidence' and giving rise to the term 'replication crisis' and the p-hacking blog Data Colada.

n0053.title: Earlier warnings
n0053.gist: Concerns about weak replication, low statistical power, and bad reporting standards were already voiced from the 1950s through the 1990s, long before the crisis was named.

n0058.title: Psychology's central role
n0058.gist: Psychology became the crisis's focal point after a large 2015 project replicated only about 36% of 100 studies, with later projects confirming roughly half fail.

n0064.title: Medical and cancer findings
n0064.gist: Medicine and cancer biology show similarly weak reliability: only about 11-44% of landmark preclinical cancer findings and in-house pharmaceutical results could be confirmed.

n0068.title: Evidence across disciplines
n0068.gist: Large-scale replication attempts across psychology, medicine, cancer biology, economics, water research, and machine learning repeatedly find many published results do not hold up.
n0068.question: Evidence across disciplines — how widespread are replication failures outside psychology? (several field surveys)

n0069.title: In other disciplines
n0069.gist: The crisis extends beyond psychology into many other research fields, as sections on nutrition, economics, water management, and machine learning go on to show.

n0072.title: In nutrition science
n0072.gist: In nutrition science, most common food ingredients have at least one study linking them to cancer risk, though significance weakens once studies are pooled together.

n0076.title: Economics replication rates
n0076.gist: A replication of 18 economics experiments found about 61% held up, but with effect sizes only two-thirds as large as originally reported, suggesting inflation.

n0078.title: In water resource management
n0078.gist: A study of nearly 2,000 water-resources articles estimated that only a tiny fraction, around 1-7%, could even in principle be reproduced from what was published.

n0082.title: In research on and with large language models
n0082.gist: Large language models bring new reproducibility problems—shifting, undisclosed, unstable systems make findings hard to repeat, prompting new reporting checklists like GUIDE-LLM to address it.
n0082.sourceHeading: In research on and with large language models

n0089.title: Survey evidence on reproducibility
n0089.gist: Surveys show most scientists have failed to reproduce others' or even their own results, yet still trust published literature, and nonreplicable papers get cited more.

n0094.title: Causes of the crisis
n0094.gist: Weak replication rates trace to publication bias, career pressure, flexible analysis choices, low statistical power, hidden context effects, and misunderstood p-values.
n0094.question: Causes of the crisis — what mix of incentives, methods, and statistics makes findings hard to replicate? (six proposed causes)

n0095.title: Historical and sociological causes
n0095.gist: Historical accounts blame the crisis on science's runaway growth, its commercialization, and the blurring of its own 'true or false' code by outside pressures like media and profit.

n0103.title: Problems with the publication system in science
n0103.gist: Flawed publishing incentives—bias toward positive results, rare support for replication studies, 'publish or perish' pressure, mathematical errors, and poor reporting standards—make nonreplicable findings common and hard to detect.
n0103.sourceHeading: Problems with the publication system in science

n0125.title: Questionable research practices
n0125.gist: Practices like selective reporting, HARKing, and early stopping exploit researchers' many hidden analytic choices to inflate false positives, compounded by outright fraud, low statistical power, and genuine variation across studies and labs.

n0172.title: Context sensitivity
n0172.gist: Some effects may be inherently sensitive to context, so that 'hidden moderators' tied to time, place, or sample explain many replication failures better than flawed methods alone.

n0177.title: Bayesian explanation
n0177.gist: Bayesian reasoning shows rejecting the null hypothesis at the 5% level does not guarantee a 95% chance the alternative is true, especially when the effect was unlikely and power is low.

n0185.title: Problem with null hypothesis testing
n0185.gist: Critics argue null-hypothesis testing fits poorly in 'soft' sciences, where the null is never exactly true and many rival hypotheses could explain any correlation, so rejecting it proves less than it seems.

n0198.title: Public awareness and response
n0198.gist: The crisis sparked public debate, resistance from defenders of existing practice, and growing calls within psychology for tougher evidentiary standards, a 'credibility revolution'.
n0198.question: Public awareness and response — how have scientists and the public reacted to exposed replication failures? (debate and backlash)

n0199.title: Public awareness and perceptions
n0199.gist: Survey evidence from Germany suggests most of the public has not heard of specific replication failures, but still largely sees replication efforts as a sign that science polices itself well.

n0203.title: Response in academia
n0203.gist: When psychologist Susan Fiske accused replication critics of 'methodological terrorism,' statistician Andrew Gelman countered that she had tolerated weak statistics and ignored errors in published work she edited.

n0207.title: Credibility revolution
n0207.gist: Many researchers frame the crisis as fueling a 'credibility revolution,' pushing psychology toward transparency, preregistration, and stricter evidence standards, alongside calls for more patient-centered medical research.

n0214.title: Reform in scientific publishing
n0214.gist: Journals and researchers are testing fixes—clearer reporting, pre-registration, result-blind review, stricter significance thresholds, and larger samples—to make published results more trustworthy.
n0214.question: Reform in scientific publishing — what changes to review and reporting could make results more reliable? (several proposed fixes)

n0215.title: Metascience and research reform
n0215.gist: Metascience, the study of how research itself is conducted, has grown to diagnose the crisis and test fixes such as preregistration and new reporting guidelines.

n0220.title: Presentation of methodology
n0220.gist: Better, more standardized reporting of experimental methods and statistics is widely urged as a cultural and institutional fix, though applying it to qualitative research raises concerns.

n0225.title: Result-blind peer review
n0225.gist: Over 140 psychology journals now use result-blind peer review, accepting studies before results are known, and this has sharply raised the share of published null results.

n0229.title: Pre-registration of studies
n0229.gist: Pre-registration requires researchers to submit their methods and analysis plan before collecting data, guaranteeing publication regardless of outcome to curb the pull toward only significant findings.

n0234.title: Metadata and digital tools for tracking replications
n0234.gist: Proposals call for tracking how often studies are repeated and whether they confirm original findings, using ratings or digital tools to log replication outcomes over time.
n0234.sourceHeading: Metadata and digital tools for tracking replications

n0238.title: Requiring smaller p-values
n0238.gist: A widely signed proposal to tighten the standard significance threshold to p<0.005 drew strong pushback, and years later neither the stricter nor case-by-case approach has become standard practice.

n0243.title: Addressing misinterpretation of p-values
n0243.gist: Even a very low p-value can be weak evidence if the hypothesis was implausible beforehand, so statisticians increasingly urge reporting a false-positive risk alongside p-values and intervals.

n0249.title: Encouraging larger sample sizes
n0249.gist: Larger sample sizes and techniques like cross-validation are urged to counter inflated effect sizes and overfitting, since small studies and many-variable models often produce exaggerated, nonreplicable results.

n0255.title: Replication efforts
n0255.gist: Funders, universities, and new databases now actively organize, train for, and track systematic replication studies across many labs and countries.
n0255.question: Replication efforts — how is the scientific community organizing to actually carry out more replications? (funding, training, databases)

n0256.title: Funding and institutions
n0256.gist: Funding bodies including the Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research and the Laura and John Arnold Foundation have committed millions of dollars specifically to support replication research and related institutions.

n0261.title: Emphasis in post-secondary education
n0261.gist: Educators now suggest methods courses have students run replication attempts rather than original studies, giving them real training while generating many independent tests of existing findings.

n0265.title: Replication database
n0265.gist: New replication databases track growing numbers of replication attempts to avoid wasted effort, while automated approaches, like a robot scientist retesting cancer-biology claims, offer a partial technical fix.

n0272.title: Involving original authors
n0272.gist: Whether original authors should help run replications is disputed, but large multi-lab collaborations now pool diverse samples and uniform protocols to test findings across cultures and settings.

n0277.title: Broader changes to scientific approach
n0277.gist: Some researchers argue replication alone cannot fix science, urging triangulation across methods, complex-systems thinking, and theory-revision instead of simple repetition.
n0277.question: Broader changes to scientific approach — should science move beyond mere replication toward other remedies? (three proposed shifts)

n0278.title: Rethinking replication's role
n0278.gist: Beyond simple replication, some researchers argue science needs deeper structural changes to how it builds and tests theories.

n0281.title: Emphasize triangulation, not just replication
n0281.gist: Researchers Munafò and Davey Smith argue that triangulating findings across differing methods, each with its own assumptions, protects against false confidence better than merely repeating the same experiment.

n0286.title: Complex systems paradigm
n0286.gist: Some argue psychology's standard linear model wrongly assumes stable, independent variables, when a complex-systems view where variables interact and shift with context may better explain failed replications.

n0292.title: Replication should seek to revise theories
n0292.gist: Replication should aim to revise and strengthen theories rather than just confirm or deny them, and open data, code, and shared repositories are seen as essential to real verification.
n0292.sourceHeading: Replication should seek to revise theories

n0299.title: See also and references
n0299.gist: A list of related statistical and philosophical concepts accompanies the article's cited books, reports, and reviews on the replication crisis.
n0299.question: See also and references — what related concepts and sources does the article point readers toward? (a list)

n0300.title: See also
n0300.gist: A list of related concepts—including base rate fallacy, data dredging, p-value, publication bias topics, and sampling bias—situates the crisis within wider debates about statistics and method.

n0320.title: Further reading
n0320.gist: Further reading includes books and articles documenting the crisis, among them Ritchie's Science Fictions and Harris's Rigor Mortis, along with academic reviews of replication design and reporting.
